steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on a US and MRI/CT image fusion system that registers images using the patient's skin surface from a 3D depth camera instead of physical markers.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Medical imaging modalities and why real-time US is fused with other modalities
2. Fusion imaging: registration and probe tracking (optical vs EM)
3. Our system: overview and the 3D depth camera
4. Hardware: EM tracking system
5. Software: segmentation, co-registration, visualisation
6. Advantages over the state of the art
7. Evaluation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Modalities
- many acquisition techniques; different tissues, settings: signal-to-noise ratio, contrast, resolution
- high resolution -> long acquisition time, unsuitable for real-time processing
- e.g. surgical tool guidance (biopsy needle insertion); cardiological imaging, ongoing monitoring of heart function
- CT, PET, MRI high-res; US real-time; helps from simple biopsy to mini-invasive tumour treatment, neurosurgery
- US drawbacks: reduced field of view, lower quality features (resolution, soft tissues)
- trend: combine real-time US with other modalities; fusion for diagnostics, mini-invasive interventions

2. Fusion imaging
- core: accurately register patient anatomy across US, CT, MR; align into standard reference system
- often overcomplicated systems for clinical use
- image fusion (Sect. 2): track US probe position, orientation, displacements in common reference system
- (i) optical trackers: several objects, high precision, but line of sight hard in interventional room
- (ii) EM: sensitive to metals, many wires (one per tracked object)
- EM systems usually require choosing markers on patient with a wand (or needle guide wire or catheter) + selecting them on preprocedural CT/MRI, or fiducial patches

3. Our system
- innovative image fusion system (Fig. 1), 3D CT/MR + real-time US (Sect. 3)
- hardware + software; seamless integration into clinical environment, esp. interventional radiology; no specific training
- 3D depth camera: 3D surface of subject as quickly as taking a photograph
- surface bridges MR/CT anatomy and US images -> fast fusion
- highly portable camera, no change to existing operating room set-up
- also: US system, simplified EM tracking system, no physical markers or fiducial patches

4. Tracking hardware
- electronic unit, mid-range transmitter, sensors tracking 3D camera and US probe
- transmitter: electromagnetic field, up to four sensors at 70 times per second
- sensors on tracked components (Fig. 1): one on US probe, one on 3D camera -> US image and 3D surface in one coordinate system (tracking coordinates)

5. Software
- tracking, surface co-registration, visualisation
- segment skin surface from CT/MRI, 3D surface overlay on patient's 3D rendering
- clinician acquires 3D skin with camera; co-registration within a few seconds + registration error visualisation (mismatches in scan area)
- after registration: MRI or CT alongside US in various visualisation modes

6. Advantages
- state of the art: depends on doctor's ability, long learning curve; ours suits less experienced radiologists
- avoids external physical markers (interesting results, but marker positioning takes time, error-prone, doesn't fit hospital workflow)
- skin segmentation general: different anatomical regions and image types
- AI-based liver shape / vessel tree segmentation need sequences not always present; image variability across series

7. Evaluation
- co-registration accuracy MR/CT vs US (millimetric error), computational cost (seconds), noise robustness, independence from operator and setting (Sects. 4, 5)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Medical imaging has many image acquisition techniques, and they let us get information about different tissues with different settings, such as signal-to-noise ratio, contrast, and resolution. Usually high-resolution imaging has the drawback that image acquisition takes a long time, which makes these techniques unsuitable for real-time image processing and analysis. For example, surgical tool guidance requires monitoring and guiding the insertion of a biopsy needle. In cardiological imaging too, ongoing monitoring of organ functional reactions is crucial for evaluating heart function. Unlike high-resolution imaging (e.g., CT, PET, MRI), US imaging allows real-time acquisition. It helps physicians in many interventional applications, from a simple biopsy to more thorough procedures like mini-invasive tumour treatment or neurosurgery. But US has a smaller field of view than other imaging techniques and lower quality of features, such as image resolution or showing and reproducing certain kinds of tissue, e.g., soft tissues. So medical imaging is moving toward combining real-time US with other acquisition modalities. This combination of images, or fusion, is used in several applications, like diagnostics and mini-invasive surgical interventions.

The core idea in fusion imaging is to accurately register the patient's anatomy in different medical imaging data, such as US, CT, or MR images, which means aligning the different acquisitions into a standard reference system. This often leads to systems that are overcomplicated for actual clinical use. Image fusion (Sect. 2) is done by tracking the position, orientation, and displacements of the US probe during the acquisition, within a reference system that is common to the US images and the other modalities. This means using probe trackers of different kinds. Probe trackers based on (i) optical technology can track several objects at the same time with high precision, but they need a line of sight, which is hard to guarantee in an interventional room. The alternative is (ii) EM technology, which has the drawback of high sensitivity to metals and also needs several wires, one for each object that is tracked. Also, EM tracking systems typically require choosing markers on the patient with a wand (or needle guide wire or catheter) and at the same time selecting those markers on the preprocedural image (CT/MRI), or using fiducial patches on the procedural (CT/MRI) image.

This paper introduces a new image fusion system (Fig. 1) which combines 3D CT/MR images with US acquisition in real-time (Sect. 3). The system has hardware and software components that are designed so the system integrates seamlessly into a clinical environment, especially interventional radiology, with a direct approach that does not need specific training. This efficient and intuitive integration is achieved by using a 3D depth camera that can acquire a 3D surface of the subject having the US exam as quickly as taking a photograph. The surface from the 3D camera bridges the 3D anatomy acquired by MR/CT and the US images, so they can be fused fast. The 3D camera is highly portable and can be brought into an operating room without compromising the existing set-up. The other hardware components of the system are a US system and a simplified EM tracking system that does not need physical markers or fiducial patches to be placed.

[Tracking hardware]
- electronic unit, mid-range transmitter, sensors for 3D camera and US probe
- EM field, up to four sensors at 70 times per second
- one sensor on US probe, one on 3D camera -> one coordinate system (tracking coordinates), Fig. 1

[Software]
- tracking, surface co-registration, visualisation
- skin surface segmented from CT/MRI, overlay on 3D rendering
- camera skin acquisition, co-registration in a few seconds + registration error visualisation
- MRI/CT shown alongside US in several visualisation modes

[Advantages]
- no reliance on doctor's skill / long learning curve; good for less experienced radiologists
- no external physical markers (time-consuming, error-prone, workflow)
- general skin segmentation; AI liver/vessel segmentation needs sequences not always available, series variability

[Evaluation]
- accuracy (millimetric), computational cost (seconds), noise robustness, operator/setting independence (Sects. 4, 5)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:

So medical imaging is moving toward combining real-time US with other acquisition modalities. This combination of images, or fusion, is used in several applications, like diagnostics and mini-invasive surgical interventions.

This means using probe trackers of different kinds. Probe trackers based on (i) optical technology can track several objects at the same time with high precision, but they need a line of sight, which is hard to guarantee in an interventional room. The alternative is (ii) EM technology, which has the drawback of high sensitivity to metals and also needs several wires, one for each object that is tracked. Also, EM tracking systems typically require choosing markers on the patient with a wand (or needle guide wire or catheter) and at the same time selecting those markers on the preprocedural image (CT/MRI), or using fiducial patches on the procedural (CT/MRI) image.

This paper introduces a new image fusion system (Fig. 1) which combines 3D CT/MR images with US acquisition in real-time (Sect. 3). The system has hardware and software components that are designed so the system integrates seamlessly into a clinical environment, especially interventional radiology, with a direct approach that does not need specific training. This efficient and intuitive integration is achieved by using a 3D depth camera that can acquire a 3D surface of the subject having the US exam as quickly as taking a photograph. The surface from the 3D camera bridges the 3D anatomy acquired by MR/CT and the US images, so they can be fused fast. The 3D camera is highly portable and can be brought into an operating room without compromising the existing set-up. The other hardware components of the system are a US system and a simplified EM tracking system that does not need physical markers or fiducial patches to be placed.

The tracking system has an electronic unit, a mid-range transmitter and sensors that track the position and coordinates of the 3D camera and the US probe. The transmitter generates an electromagnetic field and can track up to four sensors at the same time at 70 times per second. The sensors are put on the components to be tracked so their spatial relationship in the fusion imaging setup is established (Fig. 1). One sensor is connected to the US probe and the other is on the 3D camera, so the US image and the 3D surface acquired by the camera can be represented in one coordinate system (i.e., the tracking coordinates).

The software can be divided into tracking, surface co-registration, and visualisation software. The system segments the skin surface from the CT/MRI and generates a 3D surface overlay on the 3D rendering of the patient. Then the clinician acquires the 3D skin with the 3D camera, and the co-registration software does the image fusion within a few seconds, together with a visualisation of the registration error, which helps to identify potential mismatches in the scan area. When the registration is successful, the system shows MRI or CT images alongside the US image in various visualisation modes. This lets the clinician access the corresponding anatomical information and the real-time US data during the examination.

In state-of-the-art methods the registration techniques depend mainly on the doctor's ability and have a long learning curve, but the proposed image fusion is suitable even for radiologists with less experience. Also, the proposed method avoids external physical markers. Despite the interesting results with markers, they might not comply with the existing hospital workflow, since positioning the markers takes time and can be error-prone. The skin segmentation method we developed is very general and can be applied to different anatomical regions and image types. Even the new AI-based methods for automatic segmentation of liver shape or the vessel tree need sequences that are only sometimes present in the patient data set, and they have even more complications because the images vary a lot from series to series.

We tested the proposed image fusion system on different aspects: the co-registration accuracy between MR/CT and US images (millimetric error), the computational cost for real-time applications (in seconds), noise robustness, and independence from the operator and setting (Sects. 4, 5).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Medical imaging offers many image acquisition techniques, which allow us to obtain information related to different tissues with various settings, such as signal-to-noise ratio, contrast, and resolution. Generally, high-resolution imaging has the drawback of requiring extended image acquisition time, which makes these techniques unsuitable for real-time image processing and analysis. For instance, surgical tool guidance requires monitoring and guiding the insertion of a biopsy needle. Similarly, in cardiological imaging, ongoing monitoring of organ functional reactions is crucial for evaluating heart function. In contrast to high-resolution imaging (e.g., CT, PET, MRI), US imaging allows real-time acquisition and assists physicians in various interventional applications, from simple biopsy to more thorough procedures like mini-invasive tumour treatment or neurosurgery. However, US has a reduced field of view compared to other imaging techniques and a lower quality of features, such as image resolution or the revelation and reproduction of certain kinds of tissue, e.g., soft tissues. Therefore, medical imaging is moving toward combining real-time US with other acquisition modalities. This image combination, or fusion, is applied in several applications, like diagnostics and mini-invasive surgical interventions.

The core concept in fusion imaging is accurately registering the patient's anatomy in different medical imaging data, such as US, CT, or MR images, which implies aligning different acquisitions into a standard reference system. This process often leads to systems that are overcomplicated for an actual clinical application. Image fusion (Sect. 2) is carried out by tracking the US probe's position, orientation, and displacements during the acquisition within a reference system common to the US images and the other modalities considered. This implies the use of probe trackers of different natures. Probe trackers based on (i) optical technology can simultaneously track several objects with high precision, but have the drawback of requiring a line of sight that is difficult to guarantee in an interventional room. Alternatively, (ii) EM technology has the drawback of high sensitivity to metals plus the need for several wires, one for each object to be tracked. Moreover, EM tracking systems typically require choosing markers on the patient with a wand (or needle guide wire or catheter) and simultaneously selecting those markers on the preprocedural image (CT/MRI), or leveraging fiducial patches on the procedural (CT/MRI) image [1].

This paper introduces an innovative image fusion system (Fig. 1) that combines 3D CT/MR images with US acquisition in real-time (Sect. 3). The system consists of hardware and software components designed to integrate seamlessly into a clinical environment, particularly interventional radiology, with a direct approach that does not require specific training. This efficient and intuitive integration is achieved through a 3D depth camera able to acquire a 3D surface of the subject undergoing the US exam as quickly as taking a photograph [2]. The surface obtained by the 3D camera bridges the 3D anatomy acquired by MR/CT and the US images, allowing their fast fusion. The highly portable 3D camera can be introduced into an operating room without compromising the pre-existing set-up. The other hardware components of the image fusion system are a US system and a simplified EM tracking system that does not require the placement of physical markers or fiducial patches.

The tracking system comprises an electronic unit, a mid-range transmitter and sensors for tracking the position and coordinates of the 3D camera and the US probe. The transmitter generates an electromagnetic field and can simultaneously track up to four sensors at 70 times per second. The sensors are placed on the components to be tracked to establish their spatial relationship within the fusion imaging setup (Fig. 1). One sensor is connected to the US probe and the other is associated with the 3D camera, allowing the US image and the 3D surface acquired by the camera to be represented in a unique coordinate system (i.e., the tracking coordinates).

The software components can be divided into tracking, surface co-registration, and visualisation software. The system segments the skin surface from the CT/MRI and generates a 3D surface overlay on the patient's 3D rendering. The clinician then acquires the 3D skin with the 3D camera, and the co-registration software performs the image fusion within a few seconds, together with a visualisation of the registration error that facilitates the identification of potential mismatches in the scan area. Upon successful registration, the system presents MRI or CT images alongside the US image in various visualisation modes, allowing the clinician to access the corresponding anatomical information and real-time US data during the examination.

Unlike state-of-the-art methods, whose registration techniques rely mainly on the doctor's ability and require a long learning curve, the proposed image fusion is suitable even for radiologists with lower experience levels. Moreover, the proposed method avoids external physical markers, which, despite the interesting results [3], may not comply with the existing hospital workflow, since marker positioning requires time and can be error-prone. The skin segmentation method we developed is highly general and can be applied to different anatomical regions and image types. Even the new AI-based methods for automatic liver shape or vessel tree segmentation require sequences that are only sometimes present in the patient data set, and they encounter even more complications due to the high variability of the images from series to series.

The proposed image fusion system has been tested on different aspects: the co-registration accuracy between MR/CT and US images (millimetric error), the computational cost for real-time applications (in seconds), noise robustness, and independence from the operator and setting (Sects. 4, 5).
